issues.legal_issue: Retrospective legislation that restores the prior legal position and does not impair an acquired right does not violate equality merely because it affects a claimed entitlement.
material_facts: A later amendment retrospectively removed changes that had shifted the date on which surplus land vested and restored the rule that vesting occurred upon publication of the surplus-land notification.
The claimed entitlement to a higher compensation rate arose from the intervening amendment and was not an acquired right under the law that otherwise applied when the land vested.
The legislature was competent to make the retrospective changes.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective provisions were constitutionally valid and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: The legislature may amend or repeal legislation retrospectively, subject to constitutional limitations including Article 14. Retrospectivity is not, by itself, unconstitutional merely because it affects rights or expectations; the law must be assessed against the rights actually acquired. The Court applied State of Gujarat v. Raman Lal Keshav Lal Soni, T.R. Kapur v. State of Haryana, and Union of India v. Tushar Ranjan Mohanty.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_retrospectiv: A party challenged the validity of legislation that operated retrospectively.
predicates.legislature_restored_prior_legal_positio: The legislature retrospectively removed an intervening change and restored the legal position that had previously applied.
predicates.acquired_right_impaired: The retrospective law impaired a right already acquired under the law applicable before the retrospective change.

issues.definition: When a retrospective-law challenge concerns legislation that restores the prior legal position without impairing an acquired right, the law is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: A valid retrospective law containing clear deeming provisions can remove the legal basis of a court judgment, requiring the court to decide a pending appeal on the law as retrospectively changed.
material_facts: The earlier High Court judgment directed compensation to be calculated on the basis of an amendment that had shifted the deemed vesting date.
The later legislation expressly deemed that amendment never to have been made, addressed the effect of court judgments, and restored vesting on publication of the notification.
The State's appeals against the relevant High Court judgments were pending, and the earlier judgment rested on the amendment that the later legislation removed.
issues.conclusion: The Court had to proceed as if the removed amendment had never been made; the basis of the earlier High Court judgment was thereby removed, and that judgment could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory fiction must be given full effect and carried to its logical consequences, as stated in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council and followed in State of Bombay v. Pandurang Vinayak, Chief Inspector of Mines v. Karam Chand Thapar, J.K. Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, M. Venugopal v. Divisional Manager, LIC, and Harish Tandon v. Additional District Magistrate. Under Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality and Government of Andhra Pradesh v. Hindustan Machine Tools Ltd., the legislature may retrospectively alter the law and remove the basis of a judgment, but cannot simply exercise judicial power by declaring a judgment ineffective while leaving its legal basis unchanged.

predicates.appeal_against_court_judgment: A party brought an appeal against a court judgment that applied the law as it stood before later legislation.
predicates.later_law_expressly_erased_the_judgment_: The legislature expressly and retrospectively removed the legal provision on which the judgment depended.
predicates.later_law_is_constitutionally_valid: The later legislation survived the constitutional challenge made against it.

issues.definition: If a pending appeal concerns a judgment whose legal basis was expressly and validly erased by retrospective legislation, the appeal is decided under the changed law.

issues.legal_issue: A surplus-land notification remains effective to vest the land on its publication date when retrospective legislation expressly preserves its effect and deems vesting to occur only on that date.
material_facts: A notification declaring the land surplus had been published under the applicable land-reform law.

The later legislation deemed the intervening vesting amendments never to have been made and expressly provided that land covered by an already published notification vested on the notification's publication date.
The respondent argued that a fresh notification was required after the later legislation.
issues.conclusion: The original notification remained valid and vested the surplus land on its publication date; no fresh notification was required.
issues.legal_principle: The deeming provisions in sections 5(b) and 6(a) of the later amending Act required the original notification to be treated as effective and the land as vesting only upon its publication. The Court applied the principle that statutory fictions must be given their full and logical effect, as explained in East End Dwellings Co. Ltd. v. Finsbury Borough Council.

predicates.challenge_to_effect_of_surplus_land_noti: A proceeding disputed whether a previously issued notification continued to have legal effect after a retrospective change in the law.
predicates.notification_was_published: The relevant authority published a notification declaring specified land surplus.
predicates.later_law_expressly_preserved_notificati: The legislature expressly provided that land specified in an already published notification vested on the date of its publication.

issues.definition: When a published surplus-land notification is expressly preserved by later legislation, it remains effective from its publication date.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for compulsorily acquired surplus land is calculated using the rate applicable when the land vested under the law that remained in force after retrospective amendments were given effect.
material_facts: The applicable vesting date was the publication date of the surplus-land notification, rather than an earlier date attributed to the land by an intervening amendment.
The compensation rate had been reduced before the notification was published.
The respondent sought compensation calculated using the higher rate that had applied before the reduction.
issues.conclusion: The compensation had to be calculated using the reduced rate applicable when the land vested, not the earlier, higher rate.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 18(3) of the principal Act, vesting occurred on publication of the notification, and section 50 and Schedule III governed compensation. The Court applied the amendment to Schedule III made by Act 39 of 1972, which changed the applicable compensation rate before the land vested.

predicates.claim_for_compensation_after_surplus_lan: A claimant sought compensation for land taken as surplus under a land-reform process.
predicates.land_vested_on_notification_publication: The land vested in the government when the authority published the notification declaring it surplus.
predicates.compensation_rate_changed_before_vesting: The legally applicable compensation rate changed before the land vested.

issues.definition: When surplus land vests upon publication and the compensation rate changed before vesting, compensation uses the rate applicable at vesting.

issues.legal_issue: An order directing compliance with an earlier judgment does not independently determine the parties' rights when it merely enforces that judgment, and it loses effect if the underlying judgment is set aside.
material_facts: A later High Court order directed the State to comply with an earlier judgment concerning compensation assessment.
The later order did not determine any right or liability between the parties independently of the earlier judgment.
The State appealed the earlier judgment, and the Supreme Court set it aside.
issues.conclusion: The compliance order was merely an execution direction and had no continuing consequence once the underlying judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: An order that only directs execution of an earlier judgment does not independently determine rights or liabilities; its effect depends on the judgment it enforces. The Court found that the later order was in the nature of an execution order and that setting aside the earlier judgment left the compliance direction without consequence.

predicates.appeal_against_underlying_judgment: A party appealed the judgment that a later order directed the opposing party to obey.
predicates.later_order_only_directed_compliance_wit: A court issued a later order directing a party to comply with the earlier judgment without independently determining the parties' rights or liabilities.
predicates.underlying_judgment_is_set_aside: The appellate court set aside the judgment that the later order was intended to enforce.

issues.definition: A compliance order that merely enforces an earlier judgment has no continuing effect when that judgment is set aside.
